title: About
text:
I am a Master of Business Analytics student at Monash University, with a background in Data Science from the University of Canterbury.
Throughout my studies and experiences, I have developed an interest in combining analytical skills with curiosity, collaboration, and empathy to develop practical solutions to complex problems. I am interested in using data to uncover insights, understand real-world challenges, and support data-driven decision-making.
I am motivated by opportunities that connect diverse perspectives, uncover insights, and transform ideas into actionable outcomes. Through my experience with data analysis, statistical modelling, and data visualisation using R and Python, I enjoy exploring how analytical techniques can be applied to practical challenges.
I aspire to build a career where I can leverage data, creativity, and empathy to create innovative solutions that deliver value for organisations and the communities they support.

title: The Limits of Border Quarantine and the Power of Community Immunity
text:
During the COVID-19 pandemic, border quarantine strategies helped countries with low levels of community transmission and limited population immunity such as Australia and New Zealand control the transmission of the virus by limiting the introduction of infections into communities. But what happens when a new variant spreads more easily than the virus that the quarantine system was designed to contain?
The emergence of the Delta variant intensified this challenge. Even when infected travellers were isolated and tested, infections could still escape into the wider community. Understanding this risk was important for evaluating how border control and vaccination strategies could work together to prevent community outbreaks.

title: The Limits of Border Quarantine and the Power of Community Immunity
section: Higher transmissibility requires higher vaccine efficacy
text:
Higher transmissibility requires higher vaccine efficacy
When a virus becomes more contagious, the risk of further transmission following a quarantine breach increases significantly. The analysis shows that quarantine protocols calibrated for earlier, less transmissible strains may be insufficient for variants such as Delta unless paired with higher population vaccination coverage.




Table 1: Approximate vaccine efficacy (VE) required to maintain comparable modelled quarantine-related transmission risk at varying levels of viral transmissibility (\(R_0\)). The model suggests that higher transmissibility requires greater vaccine efficacy to offset the additional risk. Source: Adapted from Zachreson et al. (2022).

Table 1 summarises the approximate vaccine efficacy required to maintain a similar level of quarantine-related transmission risk under different levels of viral transmissibility. For example, when the basic reproduction number (\(R_0\)) increases from 3 to 6, the model suggests that approximately 60% vaccine efficacy is needed to maintain comparable risk. At \(R_0 = 8\), this rises to around 70%, and at \(R_0 = 10\), approximately 70%–80% efficacy is required.
These findings suggest that vaccine efficacy becomes increasingly important as viral transmissibility rises. However, the estimates are specific to the scenarios modelled and should not be interpreted as universal thresholds for safe quarantine.

title: The Limits of Border Quarantine and the Power of Community Immunity
text:
Community vaccination can delay outbreaks
Quarantine systems cannot eliminate every possibility of an infection reaching the community. Therefore, immunity within the broader community can act as an additional layer of protection by reducing the likelihood that an escaped infection will lead to a community outbreak.








Figure 1: Modelled time until the probability of a community outbreak reaches 50% (\(t_{50}\)), across different levels of vaccination coverage, vaccine efficacy, and viral transmissibility (\(R_0\)). In some scenarios, high vaccination coverage combined with high vaccine efficacy substantially delays the modelled outbreak timeline from approximately 15 days to over 1000 days. Source: Adapted from Zachreson et al. (2022).





Figure 1 depicts the modelled time until the probability of at least one community outbreak (five or more cases) reaches 50%, denoted by \(t_{50}\), under different combinations of viral transmissibility, vaccine efficacy and vaccination coverage. In the baseline scenario, this time is approximately 15 days. Under some scenarios combining high vaccine efficacy with high community vaccination coverage, it increases to around 1000 days. This illustrates how community vaccination can substantially delay outbreaks.
Figure 1 also shows that the benefit of greater coverage depends on vaccine efficacy and viral transmissibility. This means that vaccination coverage and vaccine efficacy should be considered together when assessing how well a community may withstand a quarantine breach.

title: The Limits of Border Quarantine and the Power of Community Immunity
text:
Summary
Taken together, the findings suggest that quarantine-related protection and community-wide vaccination play complementary roles. Quarantine strategies reduce the risk of transmission from imported infections, while community vaccination can delay outbreaks if infections reach the wider population.

title: The Limits of Border Quarantine and the Power of Community Immunity
text:
Limitations
The results are model-based estimates, not guarantees of real-world outcomes. They depend on assumptions about viral transmissibility, vaccine efficacy and quarantine procedures, so actual outbreaks may differ from the modelled scenarios. The results help illustrate how vaccination and quarantine can work together, but they do not identify a single best policy for every setting.
